extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners; patent prosecutors and practitioners evaluating or drafting claims under 35 U.S.C. 101
extracted.subtask_description: Interim USPTO guidance for determining whether claims meet 35 U.S.C. 101 subject-matter eligibility using the two-part Mayo/Alice framework, including a detailed procedure for nature-based products (markedly different characteristics) and examples for examiners and practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest reasonable interpretation and analyze claim as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to evaluating a claim for patentability, establish the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim and analyze the claim as a whole when evaluating for patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine what applicant has invented by reviewing the entire application disclosure and construing the claims in accordance with their broadest reasonable interpretation (MPEP 2103); analyze the claim as a whole for eligibility rather than dissecting only parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — Statutory category requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed invention (Step 1) must be directed to one of the four statutory categories: process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim is not directed to a statutory category (NO at Step 1), it is not eligible; if YES, proceed to Step 2 to determine whether it is wholly directed to a judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A — Directed to a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim is directed to a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea (judicially recognized exceptions). A claim 'directed to' an exception is one in which the exception is recited (set forth or described) in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims reciting an exception require further scrutiny because of the risk of preempting basic tools of science and technology; courts tread carefully because inventions often embody or apply such concepts. If Step 2A is NO (not directed to an exception), the claim is eligible under 35 U.S.C. 101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the judicial exception recited in the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify whether the claimed concept aligns with at least one judicial exception (laws of nature/natural phenomena or abstract ideas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are no bright lines between exception types and many concepts may fall under multiple exceptions (e.g., mathematical formulas may be abstract ideas and laws of nature). It is sufficient to identify alignment with at least one exception. Examples: isolated DNA, metabolic correlations, electromagnetic transmission (laws/natural phenomena); fundamental economic practices, methods of organizing human activities, mathematical relationships (abstract ideas). See cited case examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature-based product: decide if markedly different characteristics analysis is needed
rubrics_metrics.description: For claims reciting a nature-based product limitation, determine whether to apply the 'markedly different characteristics' analysis to evaluate whether the claim recites a 'product of nature' exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nature-based products include naturally occurring products and some man-made products essentially no different from nature. Apply the marked-difference analysis to the nature-based product limitation (or the resultant combination if multiple components) to compare to the closest naturally occurring counterpart. Do not overextend this analysis to claims that as a whole are not nature-based. For product-by-process claims, the analysis turns on whether the nature-based product has markedly different characteristics. Process claims generally are not subject to this analysis except where substance is indistinguishable from a product claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics analysis (structure, function, and/or other properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the nature-based product limitation to its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state to determine whether it exhibits markedly different characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Markedly different characteristics can be expressed as changes in structure, function, and/or other properties. Examples of characteristics considered: biological or pharmacological functions, chemical and physical properties, phenotype (functional and structural features), and structure/form (chemical, genetic, physical). Characteristics must be changes compared to nature and not inherent or independently arisen; even a small change can show a marked difference. Purification/isolation can be eligible if the resultant change shows marked difference. If no marked difference, the claim is directed to a 'product of nature' exception and proceed to Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — 'Significantly more' / inventive concept search
rubrics_metrics.description: For claims directed to a judicial exception, determine whether any element, or combination of elements, in the claim is sufficient to ensure that the claim amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception (i.e., contains an 'inventive concept').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze claim elements individually and as an ordered combination. A claim that merely drafts around an exception or adds conventional, routine steps likely fails. Every claim must be examined individually based on its particular elements; individual elements may be conventional but their combination could provide significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Considerations/examples of what qualifies as 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that may be enough to qualify as 'significantly more' when recited with a judicial exception include several types of features or results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-exclusive examples from Supreme Court/Federal Circuit decisions: improvements to another technology or technical field; improvements to functioning of the computer itself; applying the exception with or by use of a particular machine; effecting a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing; adding a specific limitation other than what is well-understood, routine and conventional, or adding unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application; other meaningful limitations beyond merely linking the exception to a technological environment. Examiners should consider these factors but are not limited to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined analysis where claim does not seek to tie up the exception
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim recites a judicial exception but is directed to an invention that clearly does not seek to 'tie up' the exception, a streamlined eligibility analysis may be appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Section I.B.3. for guidance on when full Step 2 analysis may not be necessary; the focus is on preemption risk and whether the claim meaningfully limits use of the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection drafting: identify exception and explain lack of marked difference
rubrics_metrics.description: When issuing a 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection, the rejection should identify the exception as recited in the claim and explain why the claimed product does not have markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart (if applicable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must provide reasons in the record explaining why the product is considered a 'product of nature' exception and why additional claim elements do or do not add significantly more beyond the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be fully examined under other patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Along with determining eligibility, all claims are to be fully examined under 35 U.S.C. §§ 102, 103, 112, and other applicable requirements (utility, inventorship, double patenting), and non-statutory double patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examination for eligibility is iterative and should be done in conjunction with other patentability examinations to support compact prosecution; MPEP sections (2103–2106, etc.) provide related instructions. Rejections continue to be based on substantive law and are appealable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the two-part Mayo/Alice flowchart for products and processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow the flowchart: Step 1 (statutory category), Step 2A (directed to judicial exception?), Step 2B (does claim recite additional elements that amount to significantly more than the exception?).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This two-part analysis implements the Mayo/Alice framework and promotes examination efficiency and consistency across technologies, while recognizing that variations in analysis contours may still achieve the same end result. The guidance supersedes prior MPEP sections to the extent indicated and will be iteratively updated based on case law and public feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine what applicant has invented before performing eligibility analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish what the applicant has invented by reviewing the entire disclosure to properly interpret the claim and the exception recited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding the invention is critical because courts avoid claims that would preempt others from using the underlying basic tools; this step supports correct application of Steps 2A and 2B and may justify a streamlined analysis if the claim clearly does not tie up an exception.
